analysis.one_liner: Bans government agencies from buying Americans' personal data from brokers without a warrant.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee: after introduction it was referred there on July 27, 2023 and received no further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Government agencies can currently buy Americans' phone location records, browsing history, and other personal data from data brokers instead of getting a warrant. This bill would make it illegal for law enforcement and intelligence agencies to purchase those records or obtain them indirectly, and would bar such illegally bought data from being used as evidence in court. It also requires agencies to get a real court order for data held by companies that handle communications behind the scenes, and says intelligence agencies must use the normal legal process for location, browsing, and search histories of people in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone in the United States, whose location movements, online accounts, and communications records could no longer be bought by agencies from data brokers without a warrant. People who could not have been legally surveilled directly — because the government lacks a warrant — are the main group protected, since agencies currently route around that requirement by purchasing the same data commercially.

how_it_helps.text: Bars law enforcement and intelligence agencies from obtaining customer or subscriber records — including location data, communication contents, and device data — from third parties in exchange for anything of value, and applies the ban even when the data is acquired indirectly from another buyer [S2].

Makes data bought in violation of the ban inadmissible as evidence in any court or proceeding, and requires the Attorney General to adopt procedures to minimize retention and dissemination of data acquired unlawfully [S2].

Closes a gap by extending warrant requirements to intermediary service providers — companies that deliver, store, or process communications behind the scenes for phone and internet providers — so they cannot hand over communications contents or customer records to the government [S2].
Requires agencies to get a court order, applying the most stringent applicable legal standard, before forcing third parties to hand over covered records [S2].

Makes surveillance law (FISA) the exclusive legal route for intelligence agencies to acquire location information, web browsing history, and internet search history of people in the United States, rather than leaving a loophole for other methods [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and companies selling location and personal data would lose a large customer: federal law enforcement and intelligence agencies. Agencies would have to go through the slower warrant process or go without data they currently buy.

drawbacks.text: The bill restricts what agencies can buy but does not stop data brokers from collecting and selling the same data to anyone else, such as private companies, stalkers, or foreign buyers — it targets the government buyer, not the data market itself [S2].

Law enforcement agencies argue that purchased data helps solve crimes and locate missing people quickly, and that warrant requirements can slow urgent investigations; the bill's court-order process adds steps even in emergencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but narrow: agencies would lose a fast, cheap shortcut to Americans' location and communication records, and would have to meet the same legal standard Congress already requires for directly demanding that data from phone and internet companies. The main honest objection is that the bill leaves the underlying data-broker market untouched — brokers could still sell the same sensitive data to private buyers. The bill would not have protected privacy from everyone, only from the government.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on July 27, 2023, joined by an initial group of senators from both parties [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S4].
That referral was the last action of any kind: the bill received no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 118th Congress [S4].
It drew six cosponsors, four Democrats and two Republicans [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the agencies that buy their data keep the status quo: no warrant needed to purchase Americans' location and personal records. Ordinary people get no new protection.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan at introduction — a Democratic lead sponsor with six cosponsors split four Democrats and two Republicans, including libertarian-leaning Republicans Rand Paul and Mike Lee — but no vote was ever taken, so no partisan division was recorded.

industries.note: These companies sell Americans' location and personal data to government agencies without a warrant. The bill would cut off their government sales, forcing agencies back to the court-order process.

industries.industry: Telecom and internet infrastructure companies (intermediary service providers)
industries.note: The bill adds new restrictions on companies that store and process communications for phone and internet providers, barring them from handing contents or customer records to the government. It imposes compliance burdens but strengthens privacy protections for their customers' data.
